newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss round-world balloonist says he'll try again.
newsitem.headline: Swiss round-world balloonist says he'll try again.

text.p: Swiss psychiatrist Bertrand Piccard, tearful over the failure of his round-the-world balloon bid, said on Monday he and co-pilot Wim Verstraeten were "very sad" but would be trying again.

Piccard, from a famous family of explorers of the upper atmosphere and the ocean depths, told reporters at his home that only a "stupid technical problem" had forced a ditching in the Mediterranean on Sunday only six hours into the flight.

"A human being has to dream....We'll go on, we'll try to go on," the 38-year-old balloon enthusiast said. "When we came back, I said I would check mainly with my wife. And I saw from her reaction that she agrees.

"So I think we'll go back," he added, his eyes filling with tears -- which he said were partly from frustration at seeing months of preparation ruined by a mystery leak that sent kerosene from fuel tanks sloshing into the balloon's gondola-cabin.

The 48-metre (150-foot) high craft, the Breitlin Orbiter, took off in perfect conditions early on Sunday from the Swiss Alpine ballooning centre of Chateau d'Oex, and Piccard said the balloon was "behaving beautifully."

But just under an hour into the mission, heading over Lake Geneva at some 4,000 metres (12,000 feet), he and Verstraeten noticed kerosene on the floor of the bright yellow gondola, which they wiped up with toilet tissue.

They then came down to around 2,000 metres (6,000 feet) to open the hatch of the pressurised capsule to throw out the paper and allow the fumes to escape. But after resuming their flight, the fuel began seeping in again.
"Our eyes were sore and our throats hurting from the fumes. Maybe it would have been possible to go on, but it would have been very, very dangerous," he said.
The British-built, helium-filled balloon came down off the south of France and the pair were picked up by a coastguard launch as part of a rescue operation quickly mounted by the French navy.

Mission officials said the capsule, which was recovered with them, was being brought back to Switzerland for tests to see what caused the leak of the fuel which fired hot-air burners to keep the craft aloft during night hours.
"We were very, very disappointed," said Piccard. "When I think that right now we should have been over Egypt...." His eyes filled with tears again as he spoke.
"I am a psychiatrist and I know it is not good to keep back your emotions," he said. Trying to smile. "I was not brought up to hide the way I feel."

The failure of the mission, which was to have taken Piccard and Verstraeten, a 39-year-old Belgian businessman, east across Asia and the Pacific and the United States back to Europe, was the second in a week.
Last Wednesday British tycoon Richard Branson brought his own Virgin Global Challenger balloon down in Algeria less than 24 hours after taking off from Morocco in hopes of circumnavigating the globe.

Piccard said he understood that American millionaire Steve Fossett was due to take off later on Monday from St Louis, Missouri on his second bid to become the first man to circle the globe in a balloon.
"I really wish him well," he added. But he said Fosset's task as a lone pilot on his Solo Challenger balloon would be much more difficult because he would be flying alone and in an open gondola.
"I think he is very, very courageous. He is a very brave man," Piccard said. "I don't know how far it will be possible for him to go with the material that he has."
